title: What the Instructor Emphasised in Day 3: Kubernetes, Toolchains and Architecture Styles
overview: These sketches connect Kubernetes control-plane roles, delivery-toolchain choices and application styles. Read the modernisation examples as options rather than mandatory replacements. The key architectural decisions are where durable state lives, how capability boundaries are drawn and which scaling mechanism addresses the actual bottleneck.
big_ideas: A highly available Kubernetes control plane replicates components; leader election applies to coordinating controllers, while API servers and etcd have different availability roles.
A cloud native stack is a chain of choices: language, data store, build, deploy, release, then the product.
Traditional web concerns still exist; cloud-native designs choose suitable interfaces, state stores, security and observability mechanisms for them.
Keep durable state out of individual replaceable service instances; browsers may still use cookies or tokens and shared server-side sessions can be valid.

Architectures are singular (monolith, small pipelines, IoT microkernel) or distributed (microservices, event-driven, large pipelines, microliths, Lambda/Kappa, AI-native); real systems are often hybrid.
Styles can be placed on a three-axis scaling chart: business-function decomposition, data scaling and replication.

sections.title: Kubernetes, toolchain and traditional vs cloud native
sections.summary: How Kubernetes is organised, the technology choices along a delivery toolchain, and how each traditional web concern maps to a cloud native equivalent.

notes.foot: A **blanket active-master/standby model** hides these differences.

items: **Container** = **Linux kernel isolation** plus a **runtime**, **not a VM**
**So** → Kubernetes can **pack and restart** them **so cheaply**

notes.h: The toolchain is a chain of choices
notes.foot: An architect **justifies each link**, not just the **product names**.

notes.h: Modernise each concern where it helps
items: **Agent harnesses** → add a **different kind of workflow** with **verification needs**

notes.lead: Read “cookies disabled” as a sketch example, not a cloud-native rule.
items: **Shared server-side session store** → also supports **replaceable replicas**
**Avoid** → **durable state** held **only in one application instance**

terms.def: The Kubernetes components that schedule and manage workloads across nodes.
Agent on each node that starts and monitors the pods the master assigns.
Selecting an active coordinator among replicas, as used by scheduler/controller instances; not the operating model of every control-plane component.
ReplicaSet keeps N pod copies running; a Deployment manages ReplicaSets for rolling updates.
Declare desired state in Git and let a tool such as Argo CD or Flux sync the cluster to it.

check.q: A team designs a highly available Kubernetes control plane as 'one active master and one standby master'. What does this description hide?

a.lead: Each **control-plane component** has its **own availability model**.
items: **Controllers** and **schedulers**: **leader election** → only one acts at a time
**etcd**: needs a **quorum**, usually an **odd number of members**
**Active/standby pair** → can **lose etcd quorum** or leave **API requests unserved**

check.q: A traditional web app keeps user sessions in each app server's memory and uses cookies to hold session IDs. A teammate says going cloud native means disabling cookies. Do you agree?

items: A **cookie** can still carry a **session identifier** or **token**
**The scaling problem**: **session state** that lives only on **one replaceable instance**
**Fix**: move sessions to a **shared store**, or use suitable **client-held tokens** → **any replica** can serve the next request
a.foot: The **cookie transport** and **where the state lives** are **separate choices**.

check.q: In the delivery toolchain (language, data store, build, deploy, release tracking), a team picks a vector database as its main store 'because it's modern'. The app records orders and payments. What is wrong?

items: Each **link in the toolchain** should be **justified by requirements**
**Orders and payments** need **transactions** and **integrity** → **relational** or **NewSQL** stores
**Vector store**: serves **similarity search**, for example for **RAG** → could sit **alongside** them
a.foot: **Modern options** are added **where they help**, not as **automatic replacements**.

check.q: A company wants to replace its SOAP web services and ESB-based workflows. What cloud-native options does the instructor map them to, and what caution applies?

items: **SOAP services** → **Kubernetes services** exposed through **API gateways** with **REST**
In the instructor's list, also → **agent harnesses** with **evals** and **human validation**
a.foot: **Caution**: replace **selected integrations** where **requirements justify** it, since none of these **automatically replaces** every working mechanism, and **agent workflows need verification**.

layers.label: API servers
layers.detail: Provide access to cluster resources. Multiple serving instances reduce reliance on one management node.

layers.label: Schedulers and controllers
layers.detail: Replicas use leader election for coordinated scheduling and reconciliation.

layers.label: etcd quorum
layers.detail: Replicated state needs a working majority and backups; an extra API server cannot substitute for lost state quorum.

sections.title: Architecture style classification and scaling map
sections.summary: Singular vs distributed families, where each style sits on a three-axis scaling chart, and a Netflix-style application as a decomposition exercise.

notes.lead: Application architectures split into singular and distributed families.

items: **Sketch's VM/container/function and database names** → **examples**, **not a ranking of scalability**
**Counter-examples** → a **VM can host services**, a **container a monolith**, a **relational database can be partitioned**

notes.lead: Decompose into services, each with a fitting data store:

terms.def: Instructor's term for styles deployed as one unit: monolith, small pipelines, microkernel.
Coarse-grained service between monolith and microservices.
Systems designed around AI models or agents as core components, not add-ons.

check.q: A 6-person team wants independent deployment for three areas of its product but can't operate dozens of services. Microservices, monolith or something between?

a.lead: A **microlith**: the instructor's term for a **coarse-grained deployable** between a **monolith** and **microservices**.
items: **Three independently deployable units**, each with some **independent scaling**
Suits teams without the **operational maturity** for many services
a.foot: **Split further later** if one area needs it.

check.q: A team says 'we moved from VMs to containers to functions, so we are now properly decomposed by business function'. Is that right?

items: A **VM** can host **several services**, a **container** can hold a **monolith**, and a **function** can be **one handler** inside a service
**Decompose first** by **business capability** and **operating needs**, then choose the **execution unit** for each part
**Replication** and **data partitioning** are further, **independent scaling decisions**

check.q: Decompose a streaming app's search, profile, playback-resume and title-row recommendations into services, choosing a data store for each with a reason.

items: **Search** → a **search index** or **document store**, for **text queries**
**Playback resume position** → a fast **key-value store**: **written often**, read by **user and title**
**Recommendations** → a service fed by **viewing events**, which **precomputes** the **title rows** into a **fast read store**
a.foot: Each store adds **operational cost**, so **share stores** where the **access patterns match**.

visuals.title: Choose the scaling axis from the bottleneck
visuals.caption: Database family and packaging format do not create a universal scale ranking.

exam_angles.q: Decompose a Netflix-like streaming platform into a cloud-native architecture: identify services and data stores, how viewing events reach recommendations, how it is deployed, and how it scales on each axis.

items: **Events**: **viewing events** flow through a **stream** into **recommendation processing**, **Kappa-style**
**Deployment**: **stateless services** as **Kubernetes Deployments** behind **Services** and an **API gateway**, using **tokens** or **shared session state** so **any replica** can serve

sub: **Functional decomposition**: hot services such as **playback** scale alone

a.foot: **Costs**: **eventual consistency** in recommendations and **more services to operate**.

exam_angles.q: Modernise a traditional web app that uses server-side sessions in memory, SOAP services, an ESB for workflows and a relational database. Decide what to keep, what to change and why.

items: **Keep cookies**, but move **sessions** to a **shared store** or **tokens** → **replicas are replaceable**
**SOAP** → expose its functions through an **API gateway** with **REST**; **rewrite** services only where **change justifies** it
**ESB workflows** → move toward **events** or **lightweight orchestration**, **one flow at a time**
**First**: add **observability** and **automated delivery** (**CI/CD** or **GitOps**) → they make every later change **safer**
a.foot: Don't swap in a **vector store** or **agents** unless a **requirement** calls for them.

exam_angles.q: Explain how Kubernetes provides high availability for both the control plane and the applications, and say why a large replica count alone doesn't guarantee availability to users.

sub: **Health probes** → **kubelet restarts** failed containers and **controllers replace lost Pods**
**Persistent data** with its own **replication and recovery**

items.t: **Why replica count alone doesn't help**: replicas may

a.foot: Availability must be **designed end to end**.

exam_angles.q: A new product will start with one team and modest load but expects to grow. Choose between a singular and a distributed architecture, and explain how you would leave room to evolve.

a.lead: Choose a **singular, modular architecture**: **simplicity** and **low latency** outweigh **independent scaling** at this size.
items: Make it **stateless** and **containerised** → **replication** works from day one
Keep **data ownership per module** → the parts can later be split into **microliths** or **microservices**
a.foot: Real systems end up **hybrid**, so plan the **first split** around the module most likely to need **independent scaling**.
